hook.text: Coffee first thing in the morning may actually fight your body's own natural wake-up system.

buildup.text: Cortisol—the stress hormone—peaks between 8–9 AM. It naturally promotes alertness without any caffeine.

discovery.text: Drinking coffee during peak cortisol blunts the hormone's effect and builds caffeine tolerance faster.

twist.text: Neuroscientists suggest waiting until 9:30–11 AM for coffee—when cortisol dips and caffeine has the most impact.

climax.text: Your body already wakes you up with its own chemistry. Coffee works best when it complements, not competes.

punchline.text: Let cortisol handle the first hour. Caffeine works better later.

quiz.question: Why might drinking coffee right at 8 AM be suboptimal?
options: Coffee is weaker in the morning
Peak cortisol already promotes alertness, and caffeine competes with it

details.summary: Caffeine stimulates cortisol production, the body's primary stress hormone. The cortisol spike is largest in the morning and in non-habitual drinkers. Regular consumers develop partial tolerance, but cortisol response still rises when caffeine is consumed during stressful situations.
details.whyItMatters: Cortisol spikes from caffeine compound existing stress responses. Timing caffeine intake around natural cortisol rhythms can minimize unnecessary hormonal stress.
takeaways: Caffeine triggers a measurable spike in cortisol production
The effect is strongest in the morning and for occasional drinkers
Stress plus caffeine amplifies the cortisol response significantly

faq.question: Should you avoid coffee first thing in the morning because of cortisol?
faq.answer: Some experts suggest waiting 60 to 90 minutes after waking, when natural cortisol peaks subside. Drinking coffee during the cortisol peak may blunt its wake-up effect and add unnecessary hormonal stress.

faq.question: Does regular coffee drinking reduce the cortisol response over time?
faq.answer: Partial tolerance develops with habitual consumption, meaning the cortisol spike is smaller than in occasional drinkers. However, the response never fully disappears and increases again under psychological stress.
